article.overview:
A laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) spectrometer illuminates a sample with a laser and measures the light the sample re-emits at a longer wavelength. Many organic (carbon-based) molecules absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it within nanoseconds, and that prompt emission can be separated in time from the slower luminescence of many minerals [2][3]. This makes LIF a candidate for finding and mapping organic material on rock and soil surfaces without grinding or preparing the sample [3].

*Figure: SHERLOC, an arm-mounted deep-ultraviolet Raman and fluorescence spectrometer on NASA's Mars 2020 Perseverance rover. Image credit NASA/JPL-Caltech; NASA Photojournal PIA23621 [6].*

The catalogue entry names a surface analysis instrument of this type for lunar use. The flown instrument closest to this concept is SHERLOC on the Perseverance rover on Mars, which combines Raman spectroscopy and native fluorescence on one detector [1]. Other designs, including the OrganiCam imager and a combined LIBS, Raman and fluorescence concept for a Europa lander, are at prototype or proposal stage [2][7]. No payload in the sources reviewed is documented as operating on the Moon.
article.description:
A laser-induced fluorescence spectrometer normally contains five functional parts: a pulsed or continuous excitation laser, usually in the ultraviolet (UV) or visible range; beam-delivery and focusing optics; collection optics that gather the returned light; a spectrograph or filters that separate wavelengths; and a detector, often an intensified or gated camera, that records spectra or images [1][2][3]. Some designs measure a single point, while others build a two-dimensional map by scanning the beam or the sample [3].

Two design families appear in the sources reviewed. Point-spectrum instruments record a spectrum from one small spot, as in the SHERLOC arm instrument, which maps composition over areas of several millimetres by moving the arm [1]. Imaging instruments flood a wide area with a diffused laser beam and record luminescence as a picture, as in the OrganiCam concept, which can switch to a small-spot Raman and fluorescence mode by removing the diffuser [2]. Both families have been described for combined Raman and fluorescence use, because the two techniques respond to different molecular properties [1][2].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The main purpose of a LIF spectrometer is to detect organic compounds and map where they occur at the surface of a sample. The sources reviewed present three application areas.

First, astrobiology. Storrie-Lombardi and colleagues proposed UV LIF imaging as a rapid survey tool for amino acids, nucleic acids, microbial life, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in Mars regolith, and reported field tests in Antarctica that used 532 nm excitation to detect photosynthetic pigments in cyanobacterial communities in lake ice [4]. Second, meteorite and sample analysis. Lymer and colleagues applied UV LIF to chondrules and calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions in four carbonaceous chondrites, comparing the results with Raman spectroscopy and SEM/EDS [3]. Third, planetary surface and standoff analysis. OrganiCam was designed for standoff detection of organics and biosignatures on planetary bodies, and the authors describe a possible Europa lander variant [2].

For the Moon, these applications have been proposed in general terms but no lunar science target for a LIF instrument was found in the sources reviewed. Any lunar use would need its own science case, since the lunar surface is a dry, airless, and radiation-exposed environment with regolith rather than the ice or rock contexts studied in the sources above [5].
article.operating_principle:
Fluorescence is emission that follows absorption. A photon from the laser excites an electron in a molecule to a higher energy state, and the molecule emits a photon at a longer wavelength when the electron relaxes. The difference between excitation and emission wavelengths is the Stokes shift, and the emitted light is the fluorescence signal. A spectrometer records the intensity of that emission across wavelengths, which gives a spectrum that depends on the emitting molecules [2][3].

Organic molecules often show prompt fluorescence with lifetimes of a few nanoseconds. Mineral luminescence can have different decay behaviour. A gated detector that opens only a few nanoseconds after the laser pulse can therefore suppress some mineral background and emphasise organic emission [2][3]. Lymer and colleagues used a gated CCD camera to measure decay over several nanoseconds on meteorite samples [3].

Raman spectroscopy works differently. Raman scattering is inelastic: a small fraction of the scattered light changes wavelength by an amount set by molecular vibrations, which gives a vibrational fingerprint. The two signals are both produced by the same laser and can share a detector. SHERLOC records Raman bands from 250 to 273 nm and native fluorescence from 274 to about 370 nm on one charge-coupled device, without time gating [1]. The sources do not establish whether fluorescence or Raman gives more reliable identification of a given organic compound; they describe the two as complementary [1][2][3].
article.scientific_importance:
The scientific value of a LIF spectrometer lies in finding organic material in its geological context. Fluorescence is sensitive to aromatic organic compounds, and at the best reported performance it can reach very low concentrations. OrganiCam's modelled survey imaging limit is 10 ppm for a single laser shot and 1 ppm with co-added shots, and its modelled luminescence spectroscopy limit is 10 ppb for a single shot [2]. These are model predictions at 2 m standoff, not measured flight results.

Spatial mapping adds context. SHERLOC's design is intended to produce chemical maps with a pixel size below 100 µm and to map organic and mineral distribution across rock surfaces [1]. Combining fluorescence with Raman lets an instrument report both where organic emission occurs and what molecular vibrations are present [1][2]. Lymer and colleagues argue that LIF can provide mineral and organic spectra faster than Raman, although their accessible text gives no quantitative timing comparison [3].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a laser-induced fluorescence spectrometer. The sources reviewed describe laboratory systems, a flown Mars instrument with a combined Raman and fluorescence design, and proposed or prototype standoff systems. Their laser wavelengths, optical configurations, detectors, and masses differ, so their numbers are not directly comparable. Each example below states only what its source reports. Unreported values are marked "not publicly specified" and are left null in the JSON.

examples.name: SHERLOC on Perseverance (Mars 2020)
examples.type: Flown instrument operating on Mars (not on the Moon)
examples.description:
*Evidence type: flown instrument, operating on Mars. It is not a lunar instrument.*

- Platform: arm-mounted on the NASA Perseverance rover in Jezero crater [1][6].
- Laser: pulsed deep-ultraviolet neon-copper laser at 248.6 nm [1].
- Laser pulse duration: 40 µs. Pulse energy and repetition rate are not stated in the abstract [1].
- Spot size on target: about 100 µm [1].
- Working distance: about 48 mm [1].
- Spectrograph: single diffractive-grating spectrograph covering 250 to about 370 nm [1].
- Raman region: about 800 to 4000 cm⁻¹, corresponding to 250 to 273 nm, recorded at the same time as fluorescence and without time gating [1].
- Fluorescence region: 274 to about 370 nm [1].
- Imaging resolution: 10.1 µm per pixel for the spectroscopy boresight and the Autofocus Context Imager; about 13 µm per pixel for the WATSON imager, which is a copy of the MAHLI imager [1].
- Chemical mapping: pixel size below 100 µm; up to 7 × 7 mm per arm placement; map acquisition in under 10 minutes. The abstract describes these as performance the instrument "will enable," so they should be read as design-level expectations rather than on-Mars measurements [1].
- Mass, power, detector type, and field of view: not stated in the abstract consulted [1].

*Figure: SHERLOC at the end of the Perseverance robotic arm. Credit NASA/JPL-Caltech; source page NASA Photojournal PIA23621 [6].*

examples.name: OrganiCam (lightweight time-resolved laser-induced luminescence imager and Raman spectrometer)
examples.type: Brassboard prototype built and tested; Europa-lander variant proposed; not flown
examples.description:
*Evidence type: brassboard built and tested in laboratory conditions; proposed variant for Europa. Not flown.*

- Imaging mode: a diffused laser beam with a 12° cone covers a large area at several metres; luminescence is recorded on half of an intensified detector [2].
- Spectroscopy mode: removing the diffuser focuses the beam on a small spot for Raman and fluorescence spectra from 2 m standoff [2].
- Time resolution: the instrument is described as time-resolved, using a nanosecond-gated detector to separate prompt organic fluorescence from mineral luminescence [2].
- Modelled detection limits at 2 m [2]: survey luminescence imaging 10 ppm (single shot) and 1 ppm or less with co-added shots; targeted Raman 22% (single shot) and 2% or less with co-adds; targeted luminescence spectroscopy 10 ppb (single shot) and 1 ppb or less with co-adds.
- Laser wavelengths, spatial resolution in numerical form, and mass: not stated in the accessible article text [2]. A search summary of the paper describes millimetre-scale resolution and a 3–4 kg prototype; these two statements could not be confirmed against the Applied Optics record and are not used as specifications.
- Power and environmental qualification values: not publicly specified in the sources consulted.

examples.name: Laboratory and field UV LIF imaging and spectroscopy studies (not a single instrument)
examples.type: Laboratory and field experiments with research instruments; not flown
examples.description:
*Evidence type: laboratory and field experiments with research instruments. Not flown. Instrument specifications are not publicly specified in the sources consulted.*

- Carbonaceous chondrite study: UV LIF applied without sample preparation, crushing, or cutting to chondrules and calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions in Murchison (CM2), Allende (CV3), NWA 11554 (CV3), and NWA 12796 (CK3). The authors produced two-dimensional maps, point spectra, and gated time-resolved data, and compared them with Raman spectroscopy and SEM/EDS [3].
- Antarctic field campaign: in November and December 2008, the Storrie-Lombardi team tested UV and 532 nm LIF imaging in the Dry Valleys of Schirmacher Oasis and at Lake Untersee, Queen Maud Land, to detect photosynthetic biomass in lake ice [4].
- Mars-analogue laboratory tests: the same group reports laboratory detection of PAHs doped into Mars-analogue soils. The abstract gives no numerical detection limits [4].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A lunar LIF instrument would operate in conditions that differ from the terrestrial, Mars, and ice-world environments in which the examples were tested. NASA describes the lunar surface as having a surface temperature of about 127 °C in full sunlight and about −173 °C in darkness, with only a very thin exosphere and no breathable air [5]. The surface is covered in powdery regolith and fractured bedrock. The thin atmosphere provides no protection from solar radiation or meteoroid impacts, and the Moon's magnetic field is very weak, thousands of times weaker than Earth's [5].

These conditions imply several engineering requirements, which are general considerations and are not drawn from a source for any specific instrument. The optical windows and laser exit would need protection or cleaning from dust. The thermal design would need to tolerate the day and night temperature swing. Radiation tolerance would be required for detectors and electronics. The laser and optics would also need eye-safety and operational controls that are not described in the sources reviewed. The NASA lunar-facts page does not state the length of a lunar day and night in Earth days, so no operating schedule is assumed here [5].
article.limitations:
- No lunar LIF instrument is documented as flown, flight-qualified, or assigned to a lunar mission in the sources reviewed [1][2][7].
- The only flown fluorescence-capable instrument identified, SHERLOC, operates on Mars and reports its specifications in an abstract whose mass, power, and detector values are not stated [1].
- OrganiCam detection limits are modelled, not measured in flight [2].
- Several numerical values come from search-result summaries rather than full papers. These values are not used as specifications in this article.
- Laboratory and field results on meteorites and analogue soils do not establish performance on lunar regolith [3][4].
- Fluorescence can be confused with mineral luminescence, and organic identification may need Raman data as well. The sources describe the two techniques as complementary rather than interchangeable [1][2][3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview:
A lunar surface LIF spectrometer would need the full set of surface-payload interfaces. These include Earth integration with the launch vehicle, transfer trajectory, landing delivery, deployment and sample positioning, power and data supply, thermal control, mechanical mounting, and dust protection for optics. The sources reviewed do not describe a lunar integration concept for any LIF instrument.

- Earth integration and launch: the instrument would be integrated with a lander or rover and launched on a lunar mission. No launch vehicle or mission is linked to this payload in the sources reviewed.
- Lunar transfer and landing: the instrument would be delivered to the surface by a lander. No lander has been named as carrying this payload.
- Deployment: a fixed mount or a robotic arm would position the instrument relative to the sample, as SHERLOC does on the Mars rover arm [1]. The lunar deployment method is not specified.
- Power, data and thermal interfaces: these are not specified in the sources reviewed and would depend on the host platform and the instrument design.

article.historical_significance:
SHERLOC is the most significant flown example. It is a deep-UV Raman and fluorescence instrument on the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover, and its design combines Raman and fluorescence on one detector [1][6]. Its flight demonstrates an operating UV fluorescence imaging approach on a planetary surface, though it is not a lunar precedent.

The laboratory and field work of Storrie-Lombardi and colleagues in the 2000s and 2008–2009 proposed UV LIF as a survey tool for organics in Mars regolith and tested it in the field [4]. The Lymer team's 2020 study applied UV LIF to carbon-rich meteorites as a non-destructive method [3]. OrganiCam and the LiRS concept are later designs that extend these ideas to standoff detection and to Europa [2][7]. None of these examples is a lunar mission.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- Lunar status: no lunar LIF instrument, mission, or funded lunar programme was identified in the sources reviewed.
- SHERLOC specifications come from the Space Science Reviews abstract. The full text was not read, so the labels of design and measured values could not be confirmed [1].
- SHERLOC's mass, power, detector type and field of view are not stated in the abstract consulted [1].
- OrganiCam's laser wavelengths, numerical spatial resolution, and mass are not stated in the accessible article text. The Applied Optics page is subscriber-only beyond the abstract [2].
- The Lymer et al. DOI was taken from a secondary summary, and the publisher page was not checked [3].
- The Storrie-Lombardi abstract gives no detection limits. Numbers for PAH detection limits found in search summaries were not verified and are excluded [4].
- The LiRS concept is known only from a search summary of a 2019 conference abstract. The ADS record could not be read, and its authors were not verified [7].
- Image rights: the SHERLOC photograph is a NASA/JPL-Caltech image. Its reuse terms were not checked beyond the NASA source page [6].

data_quality_notes: Lunar status: no lunar laser-induced fluorescence instrument was identified as flown, flight-qualified, or assigned to a lunar mission. All examples are Mars, prototype, laboratory, field, or concept work.

SHERLOC (Example 1): specifications come from the Space Science Reviews abstract only. The full text PDF was not read, so design-versus-measured labels could not be confirmed. Mass, power, detector type and field of view are not stated in the abstract.

OrganiCam (Example 2): modelled detection limits are from the Applied Optics record page (Table 1 as summarised there). Laser wavelengths and numeric spatial resolution are not in the accessible text. A search summary cited a 3-4 kg prototype mass that could not be confirmed, so mass_kg is null.

Lymer et al. 2020 (Example 3): DOI 10.1111/maps.13580 was taken from a secondary summary; the publisher page was not checked. The UV laser wavelength and quantitative results are not in the accessible text.

Storrie-Lombardi et al. 2009 (Example 3): the EGU abstract was read from a downloaded copy. It gives no PAH detection limits. Numeric PAH limits found in a search summary were not present in the abstract and are excluded.
LiRS (Example 4): known only from a search summary of a 2019 conference abstract. The ADS record could not be fetched and the authors could not be verified. No numeric specifications are given.

Lunar environment: temperatures, atmosphere, gravity, regolith and magnetic-field statements come from the NASA Moon Facts page. The page does not state the length of a lunar day and night in Earth days, so no operating schedule is assumed.
Lunar transportation: no lander, rover, mission or launch vehicle is linked to this payload in the sources reviewed. No compatibility assessment is made.
Mass, power, dimensions, environmental qualification and lunar thermal and power interfaces are not publicly specified for any example. These fields are null or marked not publicly specified.
